# Physiology, Nutrient Absorption

**Authors:** Eric J. Basile, Krunal Shukla, Marjorie V. Launico, Amy J. Sheer

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

The gastrointestinal tract comprises a highly specialized organ system responsible for nutrient absorption, with additional roles in waste elimination, hormonal regulation, immune defense, and neurobehavioral modulation. Extending approximately 9 m (30 ft) from the mouth to the anus, the gut facilitates the breakdown and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals, which are vital to energy production, growth, and cellular maintenance. Egestion of indigestible components and toxins maintains internal homeostasis. Endocrine signaling within the gastrointestinal tract regulates appetite, satiety, and metabolic processes. Immune cells within the gastrointestinal mucosa defend against pathogens while maintaining tolerance to commensal organisms. Neural and humoral signaling through the gut–brain axis exerts significant influence on behavior and cognitive function. Nutrient absorption is central to maintaining energy balance, growth, and cellular repair, and its disruption contributes to malnutrition, metabolic disorders, and systemic disease. Surgical procedures involving the stomach, small intestine, or pancreas frequently alter absorptive capacity, requiring careful perioperative planning and postoperative monitoring. Knowledge of the pathophysiology of nutrient absorption enables clinicians to anticipate complications, optimize nutritional support, and individualize treatment strategies.
